The strict-properness results are not correct as stated. Proposition 1 establishes equality only on the posterior support but then integrates that equality over the entire parameter space; an approximator can allocate mass outside the posterior support and still make the ratio constant on that support. Proposition 4 is also false without substantial identifiability or completeness assumptions: if x and θ are independent, any normalized q(x|θ)=r(x) independent of θ makes the stated ratio constant in θ, even when r(x) differs from p(x). Proposition 3 consequently inherits unsupported assumptions and also needs conditions such as λ>0 and p*(x) lying where the model evidence is positive.

The practical relevance to likelihood-free SBI is unclear. With a known likelihood, the loss directly supplies the log joint at every unlabeled observation and is closely related to performing variational inference there. When both likelihood and posterior are learned—the setting closer to general SBI—the paper acknowledges that strict properness fails, and the sole experiment shows appreciable variance bias and worse MMD.

Several essential reproducibility details are missing, most importantly the self-consistency weight λ and how it was selected. The paper also omits the number of independent training runs and meaning of error bars, MMD kernel bandwidth and sample counts, gradient treatment for samples from the evolving proposal q_t, training-time overhead, and code or data availability.

The ablation study does not examine central design choices such as λ, proposal distribution p_C, number L of parameter samples, likelihood accuracy, network capacity, or alternative self-consistency objectives. Statistical variability is consequently difficult to assess.

Claims of “no trade-off,” a “major breakthrough,” robustness far beyond training support, and no meaningful curse of dimensionality are substantially stronger than the evidence. Shared finite-capacity networks and optimization can create trade-offs even if idealized population losses share a minimizer, while success on a 100-dimensional diagonal Gaussian does not establish favorable scaling in structured models.

The test shift varies essentially along one simple mean-location direction, and the exact posterior map is linear. Thus, the reported extrapolation may be specific to this unusually favorable geometry rather than evidence of general robustness to model misspecification.

Overall, the central idea is promising, but the theorem gaps, transductive evaluation confound, weak posterior-level validation, and incomplete reproducibility leave the principal robustness claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important failure mode of amortized Bayesian inference and proposes a simple semi-supervised objective that can exploit unlabeled target observations while retaining fast inference after training.

The controlled Gaussian experiments are informative: they use an analytic posterior, multiple dimensions and unlabeled-set sizes, ten refits, and show large, consistent improvements well beyond the simulated training region.
The air-traffic experiment provides encouraging comparison with Stan, and the broader suite covers time series, mechanistic simulation, and high-dimensional images.
The manuscript is generally clear and provides useful architectural and hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims require correction. Propositions 1–2 ignore the possibility that q assigns probability outside the posterior support. Proposition 4 is false in general: constancy across theta only implies q(x|theta)=A(x)p(x|theta), and normalization need not force A(x)=1. The claim for arbitrary p*(x) also fails where the model evidence is zero. Consequently, the advertised strict propriety and “no trade-off” statements are overstated.

The method fundamentally requires likelihood-density evaluations. When the likelihood is learned jointly, the paper itself acknowledges degenerate self-consistent solutions, so the principal guarantee disappears. This substantially narrows applicability to likelihood-free simulation-based inference.

The neuron study evaluates only posterior-predictive reconstruction, which is closely aligned with the training loss, despite known synthetic parameters being available. The MNIST study is entirely qualitative. Neither establishes posterior accuracy or calibration, yet the paper makes broad claims about both.

Important comparisons and protocols are incomplete. There is no matched semi-supervised variational/ELBO baseline or convincing compute-matched baseline. Robustness competitors appear only on the two-dimensional toy task. In air traffic, M=15 evaluates the same countries used for self-consistency training, while M=4 and M=8 pool seen and unseen countries rather than reporting held-out generalization separately.
